h: Images · Frames · Overscan and Scrolling · Viewport and Color Scheme
x: Rendering There are two ways to get pixels out of the engine. Pick PaintAsync for occasional images, and frames for displaying a page continuously. Images PaintAsync paints the current viewport into a PNG. It returns null if there is no document to paint yet: Frames Encoding a PNG is too slow for showing a live page. Frames split the work into two steps instead, which allows a host to pipeline them: 1. PrepareFrameAsync lays out the page on the event loop. It returns null if no document is ready. 2. BrowserFrame.Rasterize turns the frame into raw premultiplied RGBA pixels. It does not touch the DOM, so it runs on any thread, while the engine already prepares the next frame. Preparing a frame also refreshes what the engine knows for hit testing. The cursor and links are then looked up without touching the DOM, which keeps pointer moves responsive on busy pages. Animated images (GIFs and WebPs of several frames) play on their own: when one in view shows its next frame, the engine raises Invalidated , and the next frame is the last one rasterized again, without a layout. An image plays from the moment it is first painted and as often as it tells, which is forever for most GIFs. The first frame of a page shows up early: only what is in the viewport is styled and laid out for it. The engine asks for the next frame right away (it raises Invalidated ), which lays out the whole page. Until then, the page below the viewport is blank, and the scroll position is not limited to the height of the page. Overscan and Scrolling A frame may be larger than the viewport: OverscanTop rows are painted above the viewport, and some more below it. The viewport starts at row OverscanTop . Scrolling is smooth and runs ahead of the DOM. Two properties reflect that: ScrollPosition is where the page should be right now, and changes without waiting for the event loop. ScrollTop is the scroll offset the DOM knows about. Until the next frame arrives, a host displays the last frame shifted by the difference, which is what makes scrolling smooth even when layout takes a while: A frame of a page with fixed or sticky boxes cannot be shifted, which is what IsScrollShiftable tells. ScrollHeight is the height of the page once measured, which allows drawing a scrollbar. Use ScrollAsync for relative changes (e.g., the mouse wheel) and ScrollToAsync for absolute ones (e.g., a scrollbar's thumb, with animate: false ). Viewport and Color Scheme Resize changes the size of the viewport in CSS pixels. Setting ColorScheme changes the answer to prefers color scheme . Both repaint the page. The screen size reported to media queries is set via BrowserOptions.ScreenWidth and BrowserOptions.ScreenHeight .

h: Pointer · Selecting Text · Keyboard · Selects · Scrolling
x: Input The engine translates input into DOM interactions. It fires the same events as a browser, and performs the default actions of the page, such as following a link, focusing a text field, toggling a checkbox, or submitting a form. All positions are in CSS pixels relative to the viewport. Pointer Member Description MovePointer(x, y) Moves the pointer without waiting. Moves are coalesced, which is what a UI should use. MovePointerAsync(x, y) Moves the pointer and waits until the hover state has been updated. PointerDownAsync(x, y, modifiers) Presses the primary button. PointerDownAsync(x, y, clickCount, modifiers) Presses the primary button for the given time in a row, e.g., 2 for a double click. PointerUpAsync(x, y, modifiers) Releases the primary button. ClickAsync(x, y, modifiers) Presses and releases the primary button. HoveredLink , Cursor The link below the pointer and the BrowserCursor a host should display. Awaiting a click also awaits the navigation it caused: Holding Control while clicking a link requests a new window, as does a link with target=" blank" . See Multiple Windows. Selecting Text With BrowserOptions.IsTextSelectionEnabled , the text of a page can be selected as in a browser. It is off by default, as the layouts then also record where their text comes from. Pressing the button and moving the pointer with it held selects the text in between; with Shift, a press extends the selection. A second press in a row ( clickCount 2) selects a word, a third one the paragraph. Control+A (or Cmd+A) selects all text of the page, unless a text field has the focus. Over text that can be selected, Cursor is BrowserCursor.Text , unless the page asks for another cursor. A page can cancel mousedown or selectstart , and user select: none keeps text from being selected. Scripts see the selection through getSelection() . CopySelectionAsync fires copy and returns the selected text for the clipboard, or an empty text if nothing is selected or the page canceled the event: Keyboard Keys are named by their DOM key value, e.g., "a" , "Enter" , "Backspace" , "Tab" , or "ArrowDown" . Keys and text are separate on purpose, just like in most UI frameworks: KeyDownAsync and KeyUpAsync fire the keyboard events and perform the actions of keys, e.g., Tab moving the focus, or Enter submitting a form. TextInputAsync enters text into the focused text field at its cursor, replacing the selected text. It works for whole strings, too. In a text field ( input or textarea ) the keys edit like in browsers. The cursor is the field's selectionStart and selectionEnd , so scripts see it and can place it: The left and right keys move the cursor, by words with Ctrl (or Alt). Home and End go to the start and end of the line, with Ctrl of the whole text. In a textarea the up and down keys go to the line above and below. Shift extends the selection, Ctrl+A (or Cmd+A) selects all of the text. Backspace and Delete remove the selected text, or the character (with Ctrl the word) before or after the cursor. Focusing a field by clicking it puts the cursor at the end of its text; tabbing into an input selects its text. Selects A select showing several options ( multiple or size ) is a list box: A click selects a row. With multiple , Ctrl (or Cmd) toggles it and Shift selects the rows from the last one clicked. The up and down keys move the selection, with Shift (and multiple ) extending it. The wheel scrolls it before the page. Any other select is a dropdown. Pressing it, or Enter, Space or Alt+Down while it has the focus, opens its list: IsSelectPopupOpen tells if the list is open. Frames from PrepareFrameAsync show it on top of the page (the image of PaintAsync does not), so a host has nothing to do for it. It stays within the viewport, opening above the select without room below. x: Avalonia Control The AngleSharp.Browser.Avalonia package provides BrowserView , a control displaying a web page. It has no native browser dependency: pages are parsed, scripted and painted in .NET. The control paints frames, forwards pointer, wheel and keyboard input, draws an overlay scrollbar, and shows the cursor the page asks for. The package relies on Avalonia only, so the application decides on the theme and platform packages. Rendering pages does not require a specific Avalonia renderer. The Simple Way Set the Source : The control creates an engine while it is in the visual tree, and disposes it when it gets detached. Nothing is persisted. The clipboard of the window is connected, and pages are told the color scheme of the current theme, following it when it changes. Source is what navigates: setting it opens another page. It also follows the page, e.g., after a click on a link. By default it binds two way, which is all it takes for an address bar. Note the update trigger, as otherwise every keystroke would navigate: The Options property configures the engine created by the control. Set it before the view is attached: The created engine is available from the Engine property, once the view is attached. Providing the Engine Host the engine yourself to go beyond a page in a box: to reuse it after the view was detached, to control its lifetime, or to bind against it in a view model. An engine provided like this belongs to you: the control never disposes it, and Options does not apply to it. To allow pages to access the clipboard, set BrowserOptions.ClipboardPlatform to an AvaloniaClipboardPlatform with the clipboard of the top level. If the assigned engine shows a page already, Source is updated with its address. Otherwise, the engine opens the Source , if there is any. Toolbar and Windows The control has no chrome. The engine has what it takes for building one: Engine events may be raised on any thread, so they are dispatched here. To open real windows for target=" blank" links, handle WindowRequested ; see Multiple Windows. Input Handling The control has to be focused to get keyboard input; clicking it does that. Shortcuts with Control or Alt stay unhandled, so KeyBinding s of the window work while the page is focused. Control+V pastes into the focused text field, Control+C copies the selected text and Control+A selects all of it (with BrowserOptions.IsTextSelectionEnabled ), and the extra mouse buttons go back and forward in the history. Namespace Hint Inside of a namespace below AngleSharp.Browser , the name Avalonia refers to AngleSharp.Browser.Avalonia . Should your code live in one, put the using directives for Avalonia outside of the namespace, or write global::Avalonia .

h: 1. Connect the Engine · 2. Paint in a Loop · 3. Draw the Frame · 4. Forward the Input · 5. Offer the Rest
x: Writing a Custom Host The engine knows nothing about a UI, so it can be displayed in any framework. This tutorial walks through what BrowserView does for Avalonia. Its source in src/AngleSharp.Browser.Avalonia/BrowserView.cs is the complete reference. 1. Connect the Engine Listen to the events of the engine, and tell it about the size of the view. Keep in mind that events may be raised on any thread. 2. Paint in a Loop Invalidated may be raised much more often than a UI displays frames. Requests are coalesced into a dirty flag, and a single loop paints while there are changes. Layout and raster overlap, which keeps a higher frame rate than doing them one after the other: A loop like this should be limited to about 60 frames per second, and restarted when Invalidated is raised. Catch ObjectDisposedException to end it with the engine. 3. Draw the Frame When drawing, shift the frame to the current scroll position, and leave out the overscan. The values to remember from the frame are ScrollTop , OverscanTop and IsScrollShiftable : Clear with white first, as the frame only covers the page once there is a document. 4. Forward the Input Translate the events of the framework. All of these are fire and forget from the perspective of the UI, but observe the tasks to log exceptions: UI event Engine call Pointer moved MovePointer(x, y) Primary button pressed / released PointerDownAsync (with the click count, for selecting words) / PointerUpAsync Back / forward button pressed GoBackAsync / GoForwardAsync Back / forward button held (its menu) History.Back / History.Forward , then GoAsync(delta) for the entry chosen Wheel ScrollAsync( deltaX distance, deltaY distance) Key pressed / released KeyDownAsync / KeyUpAsync , with the DOM's name of the key Text entered TextInputAsync MovePointer looks up the cursor and hovered link in the last frame right away, and coalesces the DOM events, so a busy page does not make the pointer lag. 5. Offer the Rest What else makes it feel like a browser: Set BrowserOptions.ClipboardPlatform with an implementation of IClipboardPlatform from AngleSharp.Io. Set BrowserOptions.IsTextSelectionEnabled , and put the text of CopySelectionAsync on the clipboard for Control+C. Update ColorScheme when the theme changes. Draw a scrollbar from ScrollPosition , ScrollHeight and ViewportHeight , and change the position using ScrollToAsync . Handle WindowRequested , and open a window with an engine from CreateWindow . Handle FullscreenChanged to show the page fullscreen while IsFullscreen , and call ExitFullscreenAsync when the user leaves the fullscreen mode of the host.

h: A page looks wrong or stays empty. What can I do? · How do I wait until a page is ready? · Why does my code throw or behave strangely when using the document? · Why does waiting for the engine hang in my code? · Why do ScrollPosition and ScrollTop differ? · How do I persist logins? · Why does a data: address show an empty page? · Does the engine run on servers without a display? · How do I make large pages paint faster?
x: Frequently Asked Questions A page looks wrong or stays empty. What can I do? Look at the diagnostics first, as many issues come from a script that failed, or a resource not being loaded: Layout and painting are done by AngleSharp.Renderer, styles by AngleSharp.Css, and scripts by AngleSharp.Js. Sites relying on the page being rendered by a client side framework are the most likely to stay empty, as a single unsupported API may stop their script. Please open an issue in the respective repository with a small reproduction. How do I wait until a page is ready? The task returned by NavigateAsync completes once the document has been loaded. Scripts may keep on changing the page afterwards. There is no general answer for when such a page is finished, so wait for what you are looking for: Why does my code throw or behave strangely when using the document? AngleSharp is not thread safe, so the DOM must only be used on the event loop. Use InvokeAsync . Do not keep elements around to use them outside of it. See Threading. Why does waiting for the engine hang in my code? The event loop is waiting for itself if an operation of the engine is awaited with blocking inside of InvokeAsync or a DOM event handler. Start the operation outside, instead. Prefer await over Wait() and Result in general. This includes tests: assertions that block while running async code (e.g., Assert.ThrowsAsync of NUnit) may hang, so use an awaited try / catch instead. Why do ScrollPosition and ScrollTop differ? Scrolling is smooth and runs ahead of the DOM. See Overscan and Scrolling. How do I persist logins? Use a ProfileDirectory . Without one, cookies and storage are gone with the engine: Why does a data: address show an empty page? Characters like < need to be percent encoded in the address. Use Uri.EscapeDataString , or LoadHtmlAsync to show markup: Does the engine run on servers without a display? Yes. Painting only requires SkiaSharp, whose native assets are included. On Linux they depend on fontconfig, so make sure it and some fonts are installed. Only AngleSharp.Browser.Avalonia needs a UI. How do I make large pages paint faster? Use the server GC in the application. Laying out a large page keeps a lot alive until it is done (the styles and boxes of all elements), which the default workstation GC copies on a single thread for every collection meanwhile; the server GC does it on all cores, and its heaps adapt to the size of the application. For GitHub's start page, the pauses for garbage collection went from about 150 ms to 40 ms per frame, for about 200 MB more memory: The first frames of a page are mostly spent compiling and optimizing code. A host shortens them by publishing precompiled code, and by not having the runtime wait for a quiet moment before it optimizes what is called often: The styles and the style maps of large pages are computed on all cores. A host that has none to spare turns this off with the AppContext switches AngleSharp.Css.DisableParallelism and AngleSharp.Renderer.DisableParallelism .

Today version v0.12 of AngleSharp has been published. Like v0.11 this is only an intermediate release before becoming officially stable with v1.0. We will be supported with everything we need to sustain development on this project, bringing it to the next level and provide first class web tooling to any .NET project. The vision of AngleSharp is now officially supported by the .NET Foundation! The long term vision for AngleSharp is provide all the building blocks for downloading, inspecting, running, and rendering standard web assets within .NET applications. AngleSharp is a .NET Browser Engine Core, which represents the basis for modern web tooling available to .NET applications in form of a .NET Standard library. The vision is too large to be fulfilled by a few people we need a strong community that desires and believes in strong web tooling for .NET. Thanks to the .NET Foundation for their support. Let's follow the journey towards outstanding web tooling in .NET together!

Just now the latest version of the JavaScript scripting extension AngleSharp.Scripting.JavaScript was released. In the new release with the version 0.5.0 a couple of bug fixes and improvements have been placed. All in all this is certainly leading the way forward. The biggest internal change is the placement of the correct prototype chain. This was on the list for quite some time. The change allows calling, e.g., Object.getPrototypeOf(document) with the result being the HTMLDocument.prototype element. Also objects such as HTMLDocument are now available on the window context. These objects are the constructor functions of their matching DOM interfaces. In most cases the constructors are just dummies, which cannot be used directly. A quite nice addition is the first API extension from the library. The ExecuteScript extension method works on document instances. It allows direct evaluation of a JavaScript snippet. The result is a .NET object, e.g., document.ExecuteScript("2+3") would result in a boxed System.Double instance ( 5 ). Similarly, a call to document.ExecuteScript("document.querySelector('div')") would return the instance of the first div element in the document. Finally, a couple of improvements to the type casting abilities have been integrated. Functions are now also accepted in form of strings (e.g., for setTimeout or setInterval ). Furthermore, for primitive types (strings, booleans, ...) the corresponding JavaScript conversion is applied. This is all done as it should be. For the way forward we will improve the extensibility and standard complience of AngleSharp.Scripting.JavaScript . With the v0.6 release a set of nasty tests needs to be passed, which all work in standard browsers. The ultimate goal is to reach the v1 milestone shortly after the AngleSharp.Core library reaches it.

Yesterday version 0.9.8 of AngleSharp has been released. There are not too many API changes and barely any breaking change so one should not notice anything. The biggest changes are the improvements in the parser, the cookie handling, and the requester. Here we managed to come up with a lot of useful improvements. Furthermore, more of the API has been opened. With the v0.9.9 release we will introduce some breaking changes that are necessary to prepare the v1.0 release. It is yet unclear if there won't be a v0.9.10. Right now, the tendency is to come up with the first stable and production ready release soon. In order to be production ready AngleSharp will separate most of the CSS into its own project (with its own versioning and maintenance). This will help in many aspects. However, we fully understand that AngleSharp is that much loved due to the fact of being complete , i.e., integrated so tightly with CSS. Therefore, a tiny CSS core will remain, which is responsible for parsing and building the CSSOM. Furthermore, the selectors will also remain in the core. This should be the best of both worlds. So what will transition to its own CSS base? Essentially, all properties. Additionally, some special rules and declarations. Finally, new stuff such as the rendering device or anything related to specific properties or media queries will be placed there. Overall this should simplify the structure in AngleSharp and reduce its size. The CSS parser will remain in AngleSharp. However, it will only return a generalized version of the CSSOM, which should be much easier to handle. Also in most cases it should be the best one to work against. The exact changes are all listed for v0.9.8 in the changelog.

Too much time has past since the last update. The current release v0.9.7 marks the beginning of a dramatic change in the AngleSharp philosophy. For all related projects the target will change with the upcoming version. AngleSharp will be fully targeting .NET core. This change is an investment in the future of .NET core. Furthermore, it should simplify the development process in the long run as the target platform is clearly defined. Another upcoming change is related to the DOM interfacing. Right now AngleSharp tries to portray the IDL from the W3C in form of .NET interfaces. To make some things (e.g., different naming conventions) possible attributes have been inserted. However, the major problem with these interfaces is the coupling they are introducing. It's not the most plugin friendly mechanism, as the overlap has always to be defined specifically. Therefore a new approach will be added, which will be applied to partial interfaces (usually marked as DomNoInterfaceObject by AngleSharp): We will use static classes with extension methods for such interfaces. These classes can then be defined in external dependencies. In C they are easily resolved via the compiler (once we have referenced the extension library and included the namespace we can use the methods). In, e.g., JavaScript ( AngleSharp.Scripting.JavaScript ) they can be resolved easily via an extension cache that is prepared with the configuration that collects all known extensions. In the long run this approach should provide a more agile basis. Now its easy to guess what is about to come: AngleSharp.Core will be split into two libraries. This is a good compromise between the previously suggested three libraries and the current state of a single library. In the end we will obtain AngleSharp.Core and AngleSharp.Css. The query selector capability will still be part of AngleSharp.Core, however, everything else related to the CSSOM will be outsourced. With the upcoming changes in mind the changelog of v0.9.7

More than two months after the release of AngleSharp v0.9.5 the new version v0.9.6 has been published. Besides some bug fixes the version focused on starting some changes regarding the final API touches and modifications. The version may contain breaking changes to anyone using AngleSharp. Two of things that will potentially break builds are concerned with API renaming (e.g., Submit becomes SubmitAsync ) and the removal of the IEventAggregator . While the former can be solved easily, the second one may actually require a little bit more time. Dropping the IEventAggregator was necessary to provide a uniform API that can also be exposed in JavaScript. Additionally, the usage of new Configuration() is highly discouraged . If you create plain new configurations no factories will be available to parser, requesters, ... a lot of components. This will result in ill behavior. I advise everyone to use Configuration.Default as the basis for any configuration adjustments. Finally, the scripting library ( AngleSharp.Scripting.JavaScript ) has been updated supporting the latest version of the core AngleSharp library and bringing some fixes and improvements. Together with some changes in the core library the experience should be much more complete right now, but there is still some way to go. The samples, demo projects, and the AngleSharp.Io extension library have been updated accordingly. They all work seamlessly together and will be unified with the release of v1.0.0, planned later this year. Thanks to everyone for their contribution!

Previously, a virtual file system for AngleSharp has been announced. This feature was essentially abandoned as it would be more appropriate in AngleSharp.Io. Finally, after weeks of delays and many discussions, AngleSharp v0.9.4 is available. There have been some bug fixes and improvements. Most importantly, these are encoding and insertion pointer fixes. However, AngleSharp v0.9.4 is in fact more than just a minor release. It could be considered a bridge release, as many internal things have been changed for the better. The upcoming version(s) will continue to walk the path enabled by v0.9.4. Features, such as the behavior of OpenAsync (delayed until embedded resources finished loading) or the virtual file system are already partially available. AngleSharp v0.9.3 is another round of minor updates. Besides a few bug fixes the CompareDocumentPosition method has been improved. It now passes all tests and works reliably. The most interesting new feature is the ability to define custom handling of entities. This can be done via the IEntityService . The GetSymbol is usually called with an entity like gt for XML or gt; for HTML. The difference between XML and HTML lies in the way that HTML handles entity errors. HTML has the possibility to use non semicolon terminated entities. The simplest way would be to use, e.g., XmlEntityService.Resolver , in a custom implementation. That way the common entities would be resolved by the already available service. The next release will most probably be a feature release again. Hopefully features such as the CSSOM improvements, factory extensions, or a virtual file system, will be integrated.

In the last days one of the remaining projects was officially launched: AngleSharp.Io . This library will provide many essential IO classes, helper methods, and DOM interfaces. A week ago the the first patch for AngleSharp v0.9.1 has been released. Besides fixing some issues the event loop model has been reworked. This will not be the last update to this mechanism. The next update v0.9.2 will focus on closing some existing issues, such as the proposed CssNode . One of the most important additions to AngleSharp v0.9.1 is the ability to filter (http, data, ...) requests. The standard requester service has been extended to provide the ability for this integration. It is therefore possible to stop unwanted requests directly without having to provide a custom IRequester implementation. Finally a remark for the upcoming releases: The service model will definitely change until v1. Right now there are too many interfaces and layers required to extend AngleSharp. Also the whole approach won't scale well once loosely coupled abilities, such as drawing or performance capturing, arrive. I believe that methods may be happier if they can just send a message, which may or may not find a listener. These messages will be very loosely coupled. At the moment I don't know if such a potential change will also affect the event aggregator, but only using DOM events may actually be a good thing. In the end the BrowsingContext itself may end up as an EventTarget , which would bring consistency across the entire library.

Let's have a look at the SLOC (taken two months ago) of the DOM part alone: From this picture alone we can already estimate that splitting the library could be benificial. We have roughly 1/3 SLOC spent on general, HTML and CSS functionality.
